options.why: Separating requests from execution distinguishes model behavior from enforced containment and directly measures whether the intended capability boundary holds.

options.text: Measure prohibited disclosure attempts that produce restricted content in the external draft, using labeled canary records and a declared adversarial test denominator.
options.why: This directly tests the confidentiality outcome instead of inferring it from citation presence, response fluency, or transport status.

options.text: Measure average answer helpfulness on ordinary scheduling requests and assume a higher score implies stronger resistance to hostile retrieved instructions.
options.why: Ordinary helpfulness does not test prohibited disclosure or tool authority, and it can remain high while an adversarial security boundary fails.

options.text: Measure input tokens per adversarial request and declare longer contexts safer because they contain more policy text explaining the assistant's restrictions.
options.why: Token volume measures resource use, not whether the tested confidentiality and action boundaries actually resist hostile content.

options.text: Count HTTP-success responses during attacks as security passes because all permission violations necessarily appear as network or transport failures.
options.why: Security failures can occur inside successful requests, so HTTP status cannot establish whether content was disclosed or a tool action exceeded authority.

questions.decision: Add explicit disclosure and unauthorized-action outcomes with declared attack denominators and expected permissions. These reveal whether the system violates security boundaries, even when requests complete normally and answers look fluent. Staging and synthetic data make the evaluation controlled; a clean result remains evidence for the tested attacks, not proof of universal resistance.

video_evidence.concept: Measure data leakage and unauthorized tool behavior directly under adversarial inputs.

questions.title: Measure first usable text at the agreed edge
questions.stem: A streaming assistant's model emits its first token after 0.6 seconds, but the web proxy buffers content for another two seconds before the user sees anything. Engineers report excellent model time to first token while users call the product slow. The service owner cares about when visible answer text begins, while separately retaining completion latency. Which metric and instrumentation choice BEST capture that experience without confusing provider emission, browser rendering, and complete-answer time?

options.text: Track browser request-to-first-rendered-answer-text percentiles, preserving upstream first-token and total-completion timings to locate buffering within the complete path.
options.why: This observes the user-relevant start of visible text and retains component evidence needed to diagnose why model emission does not reach the browser promptly.

options.text: Replace first-token measurements with average output length, assuming shorter answers necessarily begin rendering earlier under the same proxy configuration.
options.why: Output length may affect completion time but does not identify when buffering releases initial content or when the browser first renders answer text.

options.text: Report only the provider's first-token percentile because any downstream buffer affects completion latency but cannot affect the user's perceived response start.
options.why: Buffering directly delays visible text, so provider emission alone understates the experience that the service owner wants to measure.

options.text: Count successful stream connections as timely starts, even if the browser receives only headers while the answer text remains buffered upstream.
options.why: A connected stream can carry no visible answer text, so connection success does not measure the user's requested response-start experience.

questions.decision: Instrument request start to the first rendered answer text at the browser, alongside upstream first-token and completion spans. The provider's early token does not bypass proxy buffering. This extends the chapter's perceived-latency lesson by making the measurement edge explicit: the correct metric must observe the moment that the intended user actually experiences.

video_evidence.concept: Track time to first token alongside end-to-end time for streamed perceived latency.

questions.title: A swapped verdict is not missing at random
questions.stem: A pairwise judge compares two search summaries. When both presentation orders are tested, it favors the first position on many difficult cases. A proposed fix discards every order-inconsistent case and reports the remaining win rate as performance on the entire workload. Experts can adjudicate a subset, and the release decision concerns the difficult cases too. Which TWO changes best reduce position bias without hiding the population that the judge cannot reliably assess?

options.text: Use both presentation orders with blinded candidate identity, retaining each pair's order-specific verdict and reporting the fraction that changes under swapping.
options.why: Counterbalancing exposes positional sensitivity and preserves the evidence needed to distinguish stable preferences from a judge's presentation dependence.

options.text: Adjudicate a representative subset of inconsistent cases and report their coverage separately instead of assigning the consistent-subset win rate to all cases.
options.why: This addresses difficult-case exclusion and makes the judge's unresolved coverage visible rather than silently generalizing from an easier selected subset.

options.text: Discard inconsistent cases and multiply the consistent cases' win rate by the original dataset size to estimate total workload improvements.
options.why: Scaling a selected subset does not repair selection bias; inconsistent cases may systematically represent the difficult decisions that matter for release.

options.text: Always place the incumbent answer second so a first-position preference cancels its existing production advantage during candidate comparison.
options.why: Fixed placement substitutes another systematic bias for the original one and cannot reveal which verdicts depend on presentation order.

options.text: Keep candidate names visible and request longer explanations, treating persuasive reasoning as proof that any remaining order preference is harmless.
options.why: Longer explanations and visible identity do not establish order invariance, and candidate identity can introduce additional preference unrelated to answer quality.

questions.decision: Counterbalance order and retain inconsistent outcomes as a visible category for adjudication or separate reporting. Discarding them may disproportionately remove difficult tasks and change the estimand. The video suggests consistent verdicts; this novel extension qualifies that shortcut so the result does not silently become a claim about a population the judge failed to cover.

video_evidence.concept: Counterbalance pairwise presentation to expose position bias; do not mistake consistent subsets for unbiased population estimates.

questions.title: Scale grading at the right boundaries
questions.stem: A shipping-note evaluation includes exact container identifiers and a short explanation of handling exceptions. Domain experts can reliably score both but have time for only sixty cases per week. Deterministic code can compare identifiers, and a judge can be calibrated for explanation support using a rubric. The team wants broad regression coverage without losing expert authority over ambiguous exception interpretations. Which evaluation design BEST matches grading method to the property rather than choosing one method for every output?

options.text: Use an uncalibrated judge for every field and treat the larger case count as sufficient evidence that its grades are more trustworthy than expert decisions.
options.why: Volume does not establish grader validity, and automating exact fields through an unvalidated semantic judge adds unnecessary uncertainty to an objectively checkable property.

options.text: Use exact string matching for both identifiers and explanations, because any paraphrase of an approved exception should count as an incorrect answer.
options.why: Exact identifiers fit code checks, but legitimate semantic paraphrases need a support rubric; string equality would measure wording rather than explanation correctness.

options.text: Retain only the sixty expert cases and prohibit automated checks, even for identifiers with a deterministic comparison and documented expected values.
options.why: Human authority is valuable, but excluding reliable code checks needlessly limits broad regression coverage on fields that already have an objective oracle.

options.text: Use code for identifier checks, a calibrated rubric judge for explanations, and expert audits of disagreements and consequential slices while expanding representative coverage.
options.why: Each method addresses a property it can assess, while targeted human oversight checks the automated grader rather than disappearing from the evaluation process.

questions.decision: Grade exact fields with code and explanation support with a calibrated judge, reserving expert time for calibration, ambiguity, and important disagreements. Scale increases coverage only if the grader measures the right property. The chapter's automation preference is qualified here: many automated cases with an unvalidated judge do not automatically outrank a small trustworthy assessment.

video_evidence.concept: Use scalable code and calibrated model grading where appropriate, with human calibration and targeted review.

questions.title: Randomize at the shared learning boundary
questions.stem: A tutoring assistant tests two feedback styles. Teachers see all pupils in their class and routinely discuss the feedback style during group lessons, so pupils' later performance can influence one another. Assigning individual messages mixes styles within a pupil, while assigning pupils still permits classroom spillover. There are enough classrooms for a planned cluster comparison. Which TWO design changes best align assignment and analysis with the actual experience and interference boundary?

options.text: Analyze outcomes with classroom clustering and report the number of independent classrooms, preserving pupil measurements without treating every message as a randomized unit.
options.why: The assignment creates cluster dependence, so uncertainty and sample-size claims must reflect independent classrooms rather than inflate evidence through repeated messages.

options.text: Randomize every message and average results by pupil afterward, assuming post hoc averaging removes the mixed feedback pupils experienced during instruction.
options.why: Averaging does not reverse treatment contamination or classroom spillover caused by inconsistent exposure during the study.

options.text: Assign pupils independently within each classroom and ignore group lessons because the assistant's own conversations remain private from other pupils.
options.why: The scenario explicitly states a shared teaching mechanism, so private chats alone do not establish absence of interference across pupil assignments.

options.text: Switch every classroom to the other style at midday without a crossover plan, treating time-of-day differences as proof that the styles were fairly balanced.
options.why: Unplanned switching can confound exposure with time and carryover, and does not provide the stable, interpretable cluster comparison described in the requirement.

options.text: Assign each classroom consistently to one feedback style for the study, with the intended exposure period and safety intervention policy defined in advance.
options.why: Class-level consistency addresses both within-pupil switching and the stated classroom spillover rather than treating every message as an independent exposure.

questions.decision: Use stable classroom assignment and account for classrooms as clusters in the analysis. This is a novel extension of the video's conversation-level consistency lesson: here interactions cross conversations through teaching, so the assignment boundary must cover that interference. Repeated messages add observations, but they do not create independent randomized classrooms.

video_evidence.concept: The randomization unit should match the experience, preventing arm contamination across related interactions.

questions.title: Abstain on a missing effective edition
questions.stem: A standards assistant receives a question about a procedure's 2024 edition. Retrieval returns only the 2026 edition, which changes a numerical limit. The current prompt demands that every question receive a decisive answer and source citation. The assistant cites the 2026 passage but presents the number as valid in 2024. Which repair BEST targets the unsupported claim while preserving the ability to answer when the requested edition is actually available?

options.text: Increase output allowance so the assistant can provide a longer explanation of the 2026 limit without changing its claim about the 2024 edition.
options.why: More explanation does not supply the missing edition or remove the unsupported assertion that a newer limit applied during the requested earlier period.

options.text: Require edition-matched support and return an explicit evidence gap with a retrieval or escalation route when only an inapplicable edition is available.
options.why: This removes the instruction pressure to invent coverage and distinguishes a relevant-looking citation from evidence that supports the requested effective period.

options.text: Remove edition information from retrieved passages so the model no longer sees a conflict between the requested procedure year and the available source.
options.why: Hiding applicability metadata makes the error harder to detect and encourages the same unsupported claim instead of establishing adequate evidence.

options.text: Keep the decisive-answer instruction and add the newer citation more prominently so readers can independently notice that the effective year differs.
options.why: A prominent citation does not make the 2026 number true for 2024 and leaves the known unsupported temporal inference in the final answer.

questions.decision: Require evidence that covers the requested effective edition and allow a documented no-answer state when it is absent. A citation is insufficient if it supports a different time scope. This applies the chapter's abstention lesson to a plausible but inapplicable source, rather than assuming that retrieved text always provides the answer requested.

video_evidence.concept: Permit uncertainty and restrict factual claims to evidence that actually supports the requested answer.

questions.title: The examples reveal the contradiction
questions.stem: A release-note assistant follows a six-field template for ordinary changes, but creates a seventh field on rollback notes. The system rule forbids additional fields. Every rollback example includes a recovery_owner field, while the approved schema places recovery ownership inside the existing action field. Historical input replays show the same behavior with two capable models. Which initial intervention BEST addresses the evidence before declaring that the model cannot follow schemas for this category?

options.text: Switch immediately to a larger model while preserving all rollback examples, treating any short-term improvement as proof that prompt contradictions are harmless.
options.why: A stronger model may behave differently, but leaving the known contradiction prevents a clean diagnosis and does not make conflicting demonstrations a sound contract.

options.text: Increase the output cap so the seventh field can finish reliably, because the additional field indicates that rollback notes are being truncated.
options.why: The problem is an extra field rather than incomplete output, so a larger cap does not address the schema violation or the examples that teach it.

options.text: Revise rollback examples to match the approved six-field contract and replay both categories while holding model, schema, and source inputs fixed.
options.why: The category-specific contradiction is directly observable, and a controlled replay can test whether removing that teaching signal repairs the demonstrated failure.

options.text: Remove recovery ownership from the live rollback data, assuming the field disappears when the assistant has no factual information available to populate it.
options.why: This loses useful required content and avoids the representation question, while contradictory examples can still teach the unapproved field structure.

questions.decision: Repair the examples to express recovery ownership inside the approved field, then compare rollback and ordinary cases under a frozen schema and input set. The failures align with contradictory demonstrations across models. This does not prove model capacity irrelevant forever; it identifies a specific prompt defect to remove before spending effort on a model-tier explanation.

video_evidence.concept: Conflicting demonstrations can cause prompt failure even when prose instructions state the intended rule.

questions.title: Tune reasoning without losing rare cases
questions.stem: A code-labeling assistant returns one of seven fixed categories. Telemetry shows that reasoning consumes most output tokens, and a supported effort parameter is available. Ordinary cases are easy, but a small set of adversarial near-matches requires careful distinction. The owner permits an effort reduction only if each acceptance slice holds its existing floor. Which TWO steps best test the optimization instead of replacing quality evidence with an assumption about the task's short final answer?

options.text: Compare explicitly configured supported effort levels on a frozen representative suite that includes the adversarial near-match slice and its independent acceptance floor.
options.why: The experiment tests whether less reasoning preserves the decisions that matter, rather than inferring task simplicity from the short final label.

options.text: Record reasoning and visible output usage, completed-task cost, and end-to-end latency for each level before selecting a configuration that passes every required slice.
options.why: Complete measurements show the actual resource and service effect while preventing aggregate quality or visible-answer length from hiding failed rare cases.

options.text: Set an undocumented tiny thinking budget and interpret request rejection as proof that the model cannot perform the classification at lower cost.
options.why: An unsupported parameter failure tests API compatibility rather than classification quality; the scenario supplies a supported effort control for the intended experiment.

options.text: Keep effort unchanged and trim the label from two words to one, assuming visible answer compression removes the reasoning tokens that dominate spending.
options.why: Visible text length does not directly control the hidden reasoning expenditure identified by telemetry, so this misses the stated cost driver.

options.text: Use only ordinary labels in the comparison and assume the adversarial slice retains its score because its output vocabulary is identical.
options.why: The rare cases may need more reasoning despite sharing labels, so identical output vocabulary does not justify transferring ordinary-case performance.

questions.decision: Run a controlled supported-effort comparison and retain slice-level acceptance and full usage accounting. A one-word answer can still require reasoning, so output brevity does not establish that low effort is safe. The chapter motivates the lever; the release decision depends on measured rare-case behavior and actual total cost and latency.

video_evidence.concept: Use supported lower effort for simple tasks only after task-specific evaluation confirms quality.

questions.title: Respect the first batch limit reached
questions.stem: An archive has 180,000 independent requests ready for asynchronous processing. The documented batch limits are 100,000 requests or 256 MB, whichever is reached first. For this planning exercise each serialized request is exactly 4,000 bytes, envelope overhead is ignored, and MB means 1,000,000 bytes. The owner permits multiple submissions. Which minimum batch count fits both limits while retaining the asynchronous path, rather than assuming the request-count ceiling is the only constraint?

options.text: Submit two batches of 90,000 requests, because each is below the 100,000-request ceiling and asynchronous processing discounts apply regardless of payload size.
options.why: Each proposed batch would contain 360 MB, violating the independent 256 MB size ceiling even though its request count is permitted.

options.text: Submit at least three batches, because the stipulated byte limit permits at most 64,000 of these requests per batch before count becomes binding.
options.why: The size ceiling is reached before 100,000 requests, and three batches can cover 180,000 while satisfying both stated limits under the simplified sizing assumption.

options.text: Submit one batch after extending cache lifetime, because a longer prompt cache raises the serialized request-size limit for asynchronous batch creation.
options.why: Caching can affect repeated token processing but does not change the documented batch submission limits on count or serialized size.

options.text: Switch all work to synchronous calls because an archive exceeding one batch's count limit cannot use multiple asynchronous batch submissions.
options.why: The limits apply per batch, and the scenario explicitly permits multiple submissions, so exceeding one batch does not require abandoning asynchronous processing.

questions.decision: At 4,000 bytes each, the size bound allows 256,000,000/4,000 = 64,000 requests, below 100,000. Ceiling(180,000/64,000) is three batches. Real submissions must include envelope overhead and actual serialized size; the explicitly simplified exercise isolates which bound dominates rather than asserting a universal requests-per-batch capacity.

video_evidence.concept: Message batches are limited by both request count and serialized size.

questions.title: Refusal and transport failure are different events
questions.stem: After an update, an assistant produces more safety declines. Its dashboard counts only HTTP errors and therefore reports no change, because the declined requests complete with HTTP success. The deployed API documents a refusal stop reason and stop_details category; truncation has a different reason. The owner wants refusal rates by category while also detecting ordinary transport failures. Which telemetry design BEST preserves these distinct outcomes and a defensible refusal denominator?

options.text: Keep only HTTP status and estimate refusal categories from overall traffic volume, assuming successful responses contain no safety-related termination state.
options.why: The scenario explicitly documents refusals inside HTTP-success responses, so transport-only telemetry cannot measure either their rate or category distribution.

options.text: Log stop_reason and available refusal category alongside HTTP status, calculate category rates over eligible responses, and retain transport-error metrics independently.
options.why: This directly observes model refusal without conflating it with network failure and preserves a clear denominator for changes across releases.

options.text: Count every short reply as a refusal and combine HTTP errors into that count, because a single failure percentage is easier for operators to interpret.
options.why: Short answers can be valid and transport failures need different diagnosis, so combining these proxies obscures both the refusal behavior and infrastructure reliability.

options.text: Count max_tokens as refusal and ignore refusal stop reasons because the model may have declined before generating a sufficiently long explanatory response.
options.why: The documented stop reasons distinguish truncation from refusal, and reversing their meanings would systematically misclassify two operationally different events.

questions.decision: Record transport status and model stop metadata as separate dimensions, then calculate refusals over the declared eligible response population. Preserve unknown categories when instrumentation cannot interpret them. The chapter's taxonomy lesson prevents HTTP errors or output length from becoming refusal proxies, while the denominator makes the resulting rate comparable across releases.

video_evidence.concept: Refusals can be successful HTTP responses with a refusal stop reason and category metadata.

questions.title: An input screen needs a mixed-intent path
questions.stem: An admissions-information assistant receives many unrelated writing requests. A small input topic classifier can reject those before the expensive main model runs. Some messages combine a legitimate admissions question with unrelated writing help, and the owner requires that supported questions remain answerable. The classifier can return supported, unsupported, or mixed, and a reviewed routing policy exists. Which implementation BEST reduces wasted main-model work without silently dropping the supported part of mixed requests?

options.text: Route every mixed request directly to rejection because any unsupported phrase proves that the entire message lies outside the admissions service scope.
options.why: The owner explicitly requires supported portions to remain answerable, so blanket rejection trades away a stated requirement rather than implementing the reviewed routing policy.

options.text: Keep all requests on the main model and add a longer list of unrelated topics, treating prompt length as equivalent to an early routing decision.
options.why: A longer main prompt still spends main-model resources on unsupported requests and does not implement the separate supported, unsupported, and mixed routing states.

options.text: Reject clearly unsupported requests before main generation and route mixed requests to the reviewed supported-question extraction or clarification path, measuring false rejections.
options.why: This removes unnecessary expensive calls while retaining a defined route for legitimate intent and evidence about the supported work the screen might wrongly block.

options.text: Generate the full main-model response first and then classify its topic, discarding unrelated answers only after generation has consumed its ordinary budget.
options.why: Output filtering may control delivery, but it does not avoid the main-model cost that motivated an early input topic screen.

questions.decision: Place the lightweight topic decision before main generation and implement the reviewed mixed-intent branch. This keeps the optimization at input while preserving supported work. The chapter's early-filter lesson is extended with a realistic classification boundary; a low-cost classifier is useful only when its routing semantics and errors are evaluated against the actual service scope.

video_evidence.concept: Classify topic early to avoid unnecessary main-model work on out-of-scope requests.

questions.title: A quota must survive two workers
questions.stem: An assistant may create at most three reminder emails per recipient in any rolling hour. Two workers sometimes run concurrently, and each performs a read-then-send check against a shared counter. During a replay, both observe two prior emails and each sends another, producing four. The model prompt already states the limit. Which design BEST enforces the existing policy across concurrency rather than reducing the probability that the model asks for a fourth email?

options.text: Lower the model's default send preference and retain the existing counter race, accepting the quota whenever most replay runs stay below four emails.
options.why: A lower request probability does not enforce a mandatory bound and leaves the demonstrated race available whenever workers overlap.

options.text: Send both messages but remove the fourth from the audit log, treating the visible record of three emails as compliance with the reminder limit.
options.why: Changing the audit record cannot undo delivery and would conceal the exact policy violation the tool layer must prevent.

options.text: Use an atomic recipient-scoped quota reservation before delivery, with retry identity and expiry semantics that prevent concurrent workers from exceeding the rolling limit.
options.why: The enforceable check and reservation share one boundary, so two workers cannot both spend the same remaining send allowance.

options.text: Ask each worker to reread the counter twice before sending and keep ordinary non-atomic writes, assuming repeated observations make concurrent updates impossible.
options.why: Two workers can still observe the same count during both reads, so repeated checking does not create the atomic exclusion needed for the quota.

questions.decision: Reserve or commit quota atomically at the send boundary using the recipient and rolling-window policy, and ensure retries do not consume duplicate sends. The source lesson is tool-layer enforcement; this scenario extends it to concurrency, where a deterministic but non-atomic read-then-write check still fails to establish the required bound.

video_evidence.concept: Enforce side-effect rate limits in tool code rather than relying on model instructions.

questions.title: A real citation can still be inapplicable
questions.stem: A mineral-research assistant cites only URLs returned by its search tool. Auditors now find that several citations are real papers but concern a different isotope than the claim they supposedly support. A link-existence checker passes every example. The owner requires traceable scientific support rather than merely authentic destinations. Which TWO additions best address the remaining hallucination risk without pretending that retrieval alone verifies every sentence written from the retrieved material?

options.text: Replace passage links with journal homepages so auditors can locate supporting papers themselves, treating the journal's reputation as claim verification.
options.why: Reputation and a broad homepage do not establish the specific support relationship and would reduce rather than improve direct evidence traceability.

options.text: Allow unsupported claims to be omitted or marked unresolved, and add near-match isotope papers as adversarial evaluation cases for citation support.
options.why: The model gains a legitimate no-support outcome, while evaluation targets the plausible but inapplicable evidence that currently passes the authenticity checker.

options.text: Retain retrieved passage identifiers and evaluate whether each consequential isotope claim is supported by the cited passage's actual scope and findings.
options.why: This tests the scientific relationship missing from link-existence checks and makes the evidence traceable at the claim level rather than only the document level.

options.text: Keep the link-existence checker alone and require more citations per paragraph, assuming several real URLs collectively establish every asserted isotope relationship.
options.why: More authentic destinations do not ensure that any cited passage supports the actual isotope and claim; quantity cannot repair missing applicability.

options.text: Ask the model to recall each paper from memory after retrieval and accept confident recollection as independent verification of the search result.
options.why: Memory can repeat the same mistaken association and is not independent evidence that the retrieved paper supports the specific scientific statement.

questions.decision: Restrict citations to retrieved sources and also validate claim-to-passage applicability. A real URL removes one fabricated-reference failure but does not establish scientific entailment. This extends the chapter's source-grounding mitigation to a remaining semantic boundary: publication identity, isotope scope, and the asserted conclusion must agree before a citation can support the claim.

video_evidence.concept: Ground references in retrieved sources and verify that cited evidence actually supports the asserted claim.

questions.title: Sanitize examples before the shared prefix
questions.stem: A customer-support team uses historical chat excerpts as style examples in a shared prompt prefix. Names are replaced, but invoice numbers and unusual delivery descriptions remain, and an internal lookup can identify customers from either. The prefix is reused across unrelated customers. Security has determined that those identifiers are unnecessary for the style task. Which design BEST removes the cross-customer exposure while preserving the examples' teaching purpose?

options.text: Require stronger citation formatting around each historical excerpt so any customer detail copied into an unrelated conversation has a traceable source.
options.why: Traceability does not authorize disclosure and would leave the unnecessary cross-customer data inside every shared request prefix.

options.text: Hash customer names while retaining invoice numbers and unique delivery descriptions, treating the absence of readable names as complete de-identification.
options.why: Other retained fields still identify customers under the stated lookup capability, so name hashing alone does not eliminate the shared-context exposure.

options.text: Enable prompt caching for the historical excerpts and assume cached prefix content can no longer influence answers or appear in generated text.
options.why: Caching reuses processing, not authorization or redaction, and the model still receives the prefix content for generation.

options.text: Create reviewed synthetic style examples or remove identifying invoice and narrative details before shared-prefix use, checking that the intended style lesson remains intact.
options.why: This addresses the unnecessary customer information at its source while preserving the format and tone behavior the examples are meant to teach.

questions.decision: Replace the shared examples with reviewed synthetic cases or effective redactions that preserve style without unnecessary identifying details. A name-only edit does not address invoice identifiers or identifying descriptions. The chapter's leakage lesson applies to the actual information carried by the prefix, regardless of whether the examples are described as anonymous or cached.

video_evidence.concept: Real customer details in shared prompt examples create a data-leakage risk; use synthetic or properly redacted examples.

questions.title: Risk routing must recognize the relevant category
questions.stem: A warranty assistant automatically sends routine replies but routes legal disputes to a specialist. A keyword rule catches lawsuit yet misses messages that describe a formal demand through a lawyer without using that word. The legal owner has defined the high-risk category and requires review before sending those replies. Routine traffic may remain automated. Which TWO changes best implement that risk-based review boundary without replacing it with uncalibrated model confidence?

options.text: Evaluate a category classifier against owner-labeled paraphrases and near-misses, selecting a threshold and uncertain-case policy consistent with the review obligation.
options.why: The test targets the actual high-risk meaning and its false negatives instead of assuming a keyword list or confidence label establishes coverage.

options.text: Send all replies automatically and audit a sample after delivery, treating later specialist corrections as equivalent to the required pre-send review.
options.why: Post-delivery correction does not satisfy a review-before-send obligation and can expose the organization before the specialist sees the high-risk case.

options.text: Review only messages containing the exact word lawsuit and use accepted routine volume as proof that the current rule covers formal lawyer demands.
options.why: High throughput does not measure missed legal cases, and the scenario already supplies a relevant paraphrase that the exact-word rule fails to capture.

options.text: Gate sending on the routing outcome, holding high-risk and policy-defined indeterminate cases for a specialist while preserving the validated routine path.
options.why: This makes the review requirement affect the side effect rather than merely creating a label or notification after the reply has already been sent.

options.text: Send any reply whose drafting model reports high confidence, because confident wording demonstrates that the dispute falls within the routine warranty category.
options.why: Self-confidence is not a calibrated risk classification, and a confidently drafted legal dispute still belongs behind the owner's mandatory review boundary.

questions.decision: Use the legal owner's defined category as the routing target and test both explicit and paraphrased cases. Enforce the pending-review state before sending, including indeterminate cases under the approved policy. This extends the chapter's high-risk routing example beyond keyword matching: the operational control must cover the actual category, not merely one spelling of a risk signal.

video_evidence.concept: Use risk-based human review for high-impact categories rather than reviewing everything or trusting self-confidence.

questions.title: A handoff must support the next decision
questions.stem: An infrastructure assistant escalates a failed inspection to an engineer. The engineer receives the latest message, but not the evidence collected earlier, the checks already attempted, or the permission boundary that prevented a repair. Repeating those checks delays the response and risks another unauthorized attempt. The receiving team has defined a short handoff schema and can access controlled evidence links. Which THREE fields best make the escalation actionable without treating a fluent summary as verified evidence?

options.text: Include only a confident recommended repair and the final error message, omitting failed hypotheses to keep the engineer's first impression focused.
options.why: This hides evidence and prior attempts needed to assess the recommendation, potentially repeating unsafe or already disproven steps.

options.text: State the unresolved decision, urgency, and authorized receiving role, identifying which repair requires approval before any further consequential action occurs.
options.why: The engineer receives a concrete next task and its authority requirements rather than an ambiguous request to continue the assistant's prior activity.

options.text: Include attempted checks and their actual outcomes, including permission denials and partial results, so completed or prohibited steps are not blindly repeated.
options.why: This preserves investigation progress and reveals the boundary that blocked repair, making the handoff operationally useful rather than merely descriptive.

options.text: Include the affected asset, observed failure, source timestamps, and controlled evidence links, distinguishing confirmed observations from the assistant's causal hypotheses.
options.why: The receiving engineer can inspect the relevant facts and their provenance without mistaking an unverified explanation for an established incident cause.

options.text: Include the entire transcript without the defined structured fields, assuming raw completeness guarantees the receiving engineer notices every denial and unresolved dependency.
options.why: A raw transcript can supplement evidence, but alone it recreates the search burden that the agreed schema is intended to remove.

questions.decision: Send compact structured state with evidence references, attempted actions and their outcomes, and the next decision with its authority boundary. This preserves continuity without asking the engineer to rediscover the investigation. The chapter motivates contextual handoff; the schema here extends that lesson to distinguish observations from hypotheses and to prevent a failed authorization from becoming a repeated action.

video_evidence.concept: A useful escalation carries the case, attempted steps, evidence, and unresolved question.

questions.title: Contract scope is product-specific
questions.stem: A US research clinic is confirmed by counsel to be a HIPAA covered entity, and the proposed repository contains ePHI. Counsel has approved a particular API service and feature set under the organization's executed BAA, but has not approved its developer coding assistant or telemetry route. An engineer argues that the organization's existing agreement covers every product sharing the provider's brand. Which TWO actions correctly implement the legal owner's determination before allowing patient data into the proposed developer workflow?

options.text: Block ePHI from the unapproved developer route while allowing work on reviewed synthetic fixtures or adequately sanitized repositories within the existing policy.
options.why: This follows the stipulated legal boundary immediately without treating the approved API agreement as transferable authorization for another product path.

options.text: Ask each developer to approve the repository prompt personally, treating individual consent as a substitute for the clinic's scoped business-associate arrangement.
options.why: Developer acceptance does not replace the legal owner's organizational contractual determination or authorize ePHI in a route outside the approved boundary.

options.text: Document the developer tool's actual processing, storage, and telemetry services for counsel to compare with current eligible features and executed contractual scope.
options.why: The legal owner receives the facts needed for a product-specific determination instead of an architectural assumption based on brand identity.

options.text: Enable zero retention on one API setting and declare every coding-assistant and telemetry feature covered by the already executed agreement.
options.why: A retention setting does not extend a contract's product and feature scope or approve processing routes counsel has not reviewed.

options.text: Send one real patient file as a connectivity test before review, assuming a test invocation is exempt from the same processing-route restrictions.
options.why: The scenario supplies no test exception; a small trial still processes ePHI through the unapproved route that must remain blocked.

questions.decision: Keep ePHI out of the unapproved route and map the coding workflow's actual services, features, and telemetry for counsel's scoped determination. The video makes a product-coverage assertion; this case deliberately stipulates the organization's approved contract boundary instead of making a universal claim about current product eligibility. Counsel owns applicability and contractual approval.

video_evidence.concept: HIPAA eligibility and agreements apply to defined products and features, not an entire brand by association.

questions.title: Purpose changes before a cache boundary
questions.stem: Counsel confirms GDPR applies to an alumni assistant with two separate approved purposes. Shipping event badges needs a postal address; recommending online lectures needs only declared interests. The application currently builds one shared profile prefix for both workflows, including addresses, and enables prompt caching. Retention already meets the separate approved policy. Counsel has determined addresses are unnecessary for lecture recommendations. Which change BEST implements that task-specific minimization decision without assuming a cache hit eliminates processing or requiring the architect to reassess the lawful basis?

options.text: Remove addresses from shipping and lecture workflows alike, assuming minimization always prohibits a field even when an approved task actually requires it.
options.why: The owner has distinguished two purposes; eliminating a necessary approved shipping field is not required to stop unnecessary address use for lecture recommendations.

options.text: Build separate approved context projections for shipping and lecture workflows before caching, testing that lecture prompts and routine traces exclude postal addresses.
options.why: This enforces the legal owner’s purpose-specific determination without removing an independently approved shipping need or treating caching as an exemption from field selection.

options.text: Keep one full-profile prefix and enable longer caching, because repeated cached addresses no longer count as personal information processed for each lecture request.
options.why: Caching reuses processing of supplied context; it does not make an unnecessary address relevant to the lecture purpose or change the owner’s minimization decision.

options.text: Shorten retention for the shared full-profile prefix while leaving addresses in lecture requests, treating the existing storage policy as the only required boundary.
options.why: The issue is purpose-specific field necessity at request time, so changing retention does not implement the already determined lecture minimization requirement.

questions.decision: Build purpose-specific context before the cache boundary and verify that lecture requests never include the address field. The shipping workflow may retain its approved address need. This is a novel deployment extension of the chapter’s minimization lesson: permission for one purpose and cached-prefix reuse do not make the same field necessary for every other workflow.

video_evidence.concept: Data minimization limits personal data processed to what the purpose needs.

questions.title: Explain the rule application the user can contest
questions.stem: A research-access assistant tells applicants that an archive restriction applies. Its answer includes a valid policy URL but no specific rule, effective edition, or explanation of which submitted fact triggered the restriction. Archivists retain final authority and offer an appeal process, yet applicants cannot tell whether correcting a mistaken date would change the result. Which output change BEST improves meaningful transparency while preserving the archivist's decision boundary and avoiding disclosure of private internal deliberation?

options.text: Identify the effective restriction rule, the submitted fact it applies to, any unresolved assumption, and the archivist correction or appeal route.
options.why: The applicant can understand what drove the response and correct a factual error while the output keeps final decision authority with the archivist.

options.text: Provide a longer friendly introduction and retain only the general policy homepage, treating accessible tone as a replacement for rule-level explanation.
options.why: Tone can aid communication, but it does not supply the specific rule and factual relationship needed for the applicant to understand or contest the result.

options.text: Reveal a full internal reasoning transcript without checking its rule references, because detailed deliberation automatically establishes faithful policy application.
options.why: Unverified deliberation is not evidence of correct rule application, and the user needs a grounded explanation rather than private internal reasoning text.

options.text: Display a precise confidence percentage beside the same bare restriction message, assuming numerical certainty explains how the applicable policy was interpreted.
options.why: A confidence score does not identify the governing rule or triggering fact and cannot show the applicant which error could change the outcome.

questions.decision: Show the applicable rule, effective source, triggering submitted fact, uncertainty, and correction route. A valid URL alone leaves the user unable to understand or contest the application. This is a concise evidence-based explanation of the decision boundary; it does not require exposing internal model reasoning or implying the assistant holds the archivist's final authority.

video_evidence.concept: Transparency means explaining applicable rules, evidence, limitations, and routes for review.

questions.title: Discovery needs the operator and consequence
questions.stem: A regional rail maintenance team proposes an assistant to summarize equipment notes. Discovery has already established the intended business outcome, quality metric, approved data sources, cost ceiling, and processing region. Notes still say only engineers will use it, without distinguishing overnight depot staff from central specialists. Nobody has stated what happens when a summary omits a defect. Which TWO remaining discoveries most directly shape workflow and risk requirements before the team chooses a model or orchestration pattern?

options.text: Write the final prompt examples before interviewing operators, because example wording will determine which maintenance consequences the team needs to consider.
options.why: Prompt construction follows requirements; it should not define the consequences or review authority that the accountable maintenance owner must establish.

options.text: Establish defect-omission consequences and the accountable review or escalation policy before a summary can influence a maintenance decision.
options.why: The harm and authority boundary determine acceptable error handling and validation requirements rather than leaving risk tolerance implicit in model choice.

options.text: Observe depot and specialist tasks, documenting when summaries are consumed, available devices, peak volume, and how each role acts on the information.
options.why: Actual workflow evidence replaces a vague user label with requirements that can shape response time, presentation, capacity, and integration decisions.

options.text: Select the number of workers for each depot now and treat the orchestration graph as the missing description of how engineers perform their jobs.
options.why: A worker graph is a proposed implementation and cannot substitute for observing the human workflow it is supposed to support.

options.text: Choose the newest model tier and assume its benchmark rank supplies the missing local risk tolerance and operational user requirements.
options.why: General capability rankings do not describe the depot's workflow or decide the consequences and authority for a missed maintenance defect.

questions.decision: Observe the distinct users and decision windows, then agree omission consequences, review authority, and acceptance obligations with the responsible owner. The existing notes already cover other discovery categories. These missing facts determine whether a useful summary can be consumed in time and what must happen before someone relies on a potentially incomplete account.

video_evidence.concept: Structured discovery includes actual users and workflow, plus error consequences and review authority.

questions.title: A high-value idea can remain unready
questions.stem: A charity has three assistant proposals and capacity for one initial pilot. Volunteer FAQ drafting has moderate estimated value, licensed material, a responsible owner, and a measurable acceptance rubric. Donor relationship prediction has a higher estimated value but unresolved data rights and no identified outcome owner. Internal meeting-note classification is ready but has negligible operational benefit. Which prioritization BEST applies value and feasibility together without treating a roadmap ranking as permission to ignore unresolved prerequisites?

options.text: Pilot volunteer FAQ drafting with its acceptance rubric, while assigning a separate discovery action to resolve donor-prediction rights and ownership before reconsideration.
options.why: This selects meaningful attainable value now and keeps the higher-value but unready proposal visible with concrete prerequisites rather than treating it as launchable.

options.text: Start donor prediction because its estimated benefit is highest, deferring data rights and ownership decisions until the model prototype demonstrates attractive outputs.
options.why: The unresolved prerequisites affect feasibility and authority now; a compelling prototype does not establish rights or supply an accountable outcome owner.

options.text: Start meeting-note classification solely because it is easiest, treating any completed pilot as equally strong evidence for the charity's operational value case.
options.why: Ease matters, but negligible benefit weakens the value case compared with another ready proposal that addresses a meaningful operational need.

options.text: Build one shared agent for all three proposals immediately, assuming a common model removes the need to assess their distinct rights, owners, and acceptance criteria.
options.why: A common model does not resolve different data or ownership prerequisites and spreads the initial scope beyond the single-pilot capacity constraint.

questions.decision: Start the bounded FAQ pilot because it combines meaningful value with current readiness, and assign owners to resolve the prediction proposal's prerequisites. Its higher estimated value can justify further discovery without justifying immediate build. Readiness and benefit are distinct dimensions; neither the highest headline value nor the easiest low-value task alone defines a sound initial priority.

video_evidence.concept: Prioritize discovery use cases by both business value and feasibility rather than building every idea at once.

questions.title: Operators need the failure transitions
questions.stem: An architect must brief the platform team that will run a document assistant. The team already received the board's business case and legal's processing-scope review. Operators now need to accept on-call ownership. A proposed presentation repeats projected savings and a polished normal-path diagram but omits queue behavior, retry boundaries, and who can disable a bad retrieval release. Which presentation BEST meets this audience's immediate decision need?

options.text: Present only the legal processing review, assuming approved data routes automatically establish retry safety, queue recovery, and on-call escalation arrangements.
options.why: Processing eligibility and operational recovery are different obligations; the legal review does not supply the interfaces and responsibilities this team must accept.

options.text: Show final answer examples and user satisfaction quotes, using successful output as proof that no additional operational explanation is needed.
options.why: Good examples demonstrate useful behavior but do not explain how the team handles failures, load, or a faulty retrieval deployment.

options.text: Walk through normal and failed request paths, queue and retry contracts, release-disable authority, alert ownership, and expected load using a concrete incident exercise.
options.why: This gives the receiving team the architecture and operational obligations needed to assess on-call readiness rather than repeating information designed for other audiences.

options.text: Lead with projected labor savings and defer failure behavior until after launch, because platform engineers can infer recovery ownership from the normal-path diagram.
options.why: Business value does not establish run readiness, and authority to disable releases cannot safely be inferred from a diagram that omits that decision boundary.

questions.decision: Center the briefing on runtime interfaces and failure transitions, including recovery authority and expected operating load. The platform team must decide whether it can run the service, so the relevant evidence differs from the already supplied board case. A clear normal-path diagram remains useful when connected to the concrete incidents and controls operators will own.

video_evidence.concept: Tailor engineering communication to architecture, interfaces, and operational burden.

questions.title: Consequences belong beside the chosen benefit
questions.stem: An ADR chooses retrieval over always including a full maintenance manual. It records lower token use and faster ordinary answers, but omits that retrieval occasionally misses cross-references needed for unusual repairs. The acceptance owner permits those cases to escalate rather than receive incomplete advice. A future maintainer reading only the benefits might remove that escalation path. Which addition BEST preserves the actual trade-off the team accepted?

options.text: Document missed-cross-reference risk, required escalation and its operating cost, plus the measured assumptions and conditions that should trigger reconsidering the retrieval choice.
options.why: This captures the accepted downside and compensating behavior, making the escalation's architectural purpose visible to future maintainers.

options.text: Record only that stakeholders approved retrieval, treating approval as a permanent substitute for explaining the assumptions and quality trade-off they accepted.
options.why: Approval without reasons does not tell future readers what was accepted or when changed evidence should cause them to revisit the architecture.

options.text: Add more examples of ordinary latency savings while keeping unusual repairs outside the record, because rare failures would distract from the chosen decision.
options.why: The omitted failure mode is precisely why escalation remains required; additional benefit examples cannot preserve that consequence or its accepted control.

options.text: List individual engineers who preferred full context without documenting the missed-cross-reference behavior, because dissenting names provide sufficient future decision context.
options.why: People's positions do not explain the design consequence or required escalation path, and they cannot replace evidence about the accepted trade-off.

questions.decision: Record the evidence-loss risk, compensating escalation behavior, its cost, and the conditions for revisiting retrieval. The ADR must describe the chosen design's consequences, not merely advertise its savings. That gives future maintainers enough context to distinguish an inconvenient workaround from a control that makes the accepted architecture meet its real quality boundary.

video_evidence.concept: Decision records include consequences, including disadvantages accepted with the chosen architecture.

questions.title: Scope exclusions need a useful destination
questions.stem: A campus assistant answers library access questions. Students also ask about disciplinary appeals, which remain outside the approved service and are owned by a separate office. The SLA currently promises helpful answers without defining scope, and staff log every appeal handoff as an assistant outage. Product wants accurate service reporting and a useful student experience without adding unreviewed appeal advice. Which TWO changes best repair expectations and feedback handling together?

options.text: Classify compliant appeal handoffs separately from in-scope outages, while tracking broken destinations and misrouted library questions as actionable feedback.
options.why: Reporting now reflects intended service behavior without concealing real routing defects or incorrectly treating every permitted handoff as an availability failure.

options.text: Define library support and disciplinary exclusions explicitly in the SLA and interface, including the responsible appeal office and a tested contact route.
options.why: Students receive an understandable boundary and useful next step instead of vague helpfulness or unsupported advice beyond the assistant's approved scope.

options.text: Delete all excluded-topic feedback from the reporting system, assuming an out-of-scope request can never expose a meaningful product or routing failure.
options.why: Excluded questions can reveal broken destinations or misunderstood scope, so deleting feedback would conceal legitimate usability and routing issues.

options.text: Add appeal advice immediately to reduce handoff counts, reusing library evaluations because the same conversational interface presents both subjects.
options.why: Expanding authority changes the service and requires its own review and acceptance evidence; lower handoff volume does not establish appropriate appeal advice.

options.text: Keep the vague SLA but call every successful HTTP response compliant, whether it contains library advice, an appeal guess, or an unusable referral.
options.why: Transport success does not establish the service outcome, and this metric would hide both unauthorized advice and failed handoffs.

questions.decision: Define the supported service and measure compliant handoffs separately from unavailable supported functions. Give students an accurate destination for excluded appeals, with ownership and feedback routing. The chapter's scope lesson is extended into reporting semantics: an intentional boundary should neither appear as an outage nor become an excuse to ignore failed or unusable handoffs.

video_evidence.concept: Define out-of-scope topics and a routing path in service expectations.

questions.title: Two clocks cannot define one promise
questions.stem: A vendor reports that an assistant meets a three-second p95 completion SLO measured from backend acceptance to final model token. The customer measures browser click to usable rendered answer, including upload and queue delay, over business hours only. Both figures are technically correct for their own populations. The contract does not define the boundary, window, or treatment of timed-out requests. Which action BEST creates a durable shared service measurement before either party declares the other party's result invalid?

options.text: Accept the vendor metric permanently because the backend is closer to inference, treating browser upload and queue time as irrelevant without changing the contract.
options.why: Proximity to inference does not decide the user's service boundary, and the unresolved contract leaves both measurement populations plausible.

options.text: Accept the browser figure alone because customers pay, while leaving timeouts and business-hour selection unspecified for later monthly reporting.
options.why: Customer preference may inform the target, but unspecified population and timeout rules would allow the same dispute to recur under a different traffic mix.

options.text: Average both reported p95 values and use that number as the shared percentile, assuming averaging resolves differences between measurement boundaries.
options.why: Percentiles from different populations and intervals cannot be combined into a defensible common service percentile through simple averaging.

options.text: Define start and completion events, eligible traffic window, timeout treatment, and percentile method jointly, then validate correlated sample traces against the shared contract.
options.why: This makes the service claim reproducible and resolves the underlying mismatch instead of choosing between two legitimately different measurements.

questions.decision: Agree the experience boundary and eligible population, including timeouts, then implement correlated measurements and a shared calculation window. The existing reports measure different quantities, so choosing one party's number does not resolve the specification gap. Retaining component measurements supports diagnosis after both sides agree on the actual contractual outcome and denominator.

video_evidence.concept: An SLO requires an agreed measurement point, population, time window, and method.

questions.title: Review documentation with the behavior it describes
questions.stem: A retrieval release replaces an index alias, adds a new stale-index alert, and changes the rollback command. Code review checks the implementation, but the release guide still describes the old alias and an alert that no longer fires. Operators discover the mismatch only during an incident. The team already stores operational documentation in the repository. Which change BEST makes future documentation updates follow the relevant implementation change rather than rely on occasional cleanup?

options.text: Keep documentation in the repository but review it only every quarter, assuming version control itself guarantees that operational instructions match each release.
options.why: Version control records stale text just as reliably as current text; periodic review can leave multiple releases operating under incorrect recovery instructions.

options.text: Require affected operational documents in the same PR as alias, alert, and rollback changes, with a receiving-operator check against the rehearsed release behavior.
options.why: This binds documentation review to the concrete behavior change and verifies the instructions with the people expected to use them during recovery.

options.text: Assign all corrections to the original architect after launch, allowing implementation PRs to merge without naming which operational instructions they invalidate.
options.why: A single person's later cleanup is disconnected from the change and leaves operators exposed before correction, especially if ownership or availability changes.

options.text: Generate the guide from a normal-path diagram alone and omit commands, because operators can derive rollback steps from current code during an incident.
options.why: A diagram does not supply tested execution details, and deriving recovery under incident pressure recreates the missing operational guidance rather than fixing it.

questions.decision: Make the behavior-changing PR include the corresponding diagram, alert, and rollback updates, with an owner verifying them in rehearsal. Repository location alone does not keep documents accurate. The chapter's same-change principle connects the reviewed implementation to the instructions operators will execute, preserving a versioned record of both the system and its recovery path.

video_evidence.concept: Keep documentation with code and update it in the same reviewed change.

questions.title: A narrow pilot still needs its acceptance gate
questions.stem: A prototype classifies historical permit notes well in an executive demonstration. Product proposes a limited live pilot involving only one office and calls it equivalent to passing evaluation. The agreed acceptance plan includes rare-language cases, unauthorized-access attempts, and a tested handoff when evidence is missing; none appeared in the demonstration. The owner allows a pilot after those minimum gates pass. Which lifecycle decision BEST respects the already agreed transition without demanding unnecessary rediscovery?

options.text: Run the agreed rare-language, access-boundary, and evidence-gap checks, resolve failures, and rehearse the receiving office's handoff before enabling the permitted pilot.
options.why: This completes the existing transition criteria and retains the pilot's legitimate role in observing operation after minimum readiness is established.

options.text: Repeat the executive demonstration with more ordinary examples and use audience approval as evidence that the rare-language and handoff criteria now pass.
options.why: Ordinary examples and audience approval do not exercise the specified difficult slices, authorization attempts, or operational handoff conditions.

options.text: Restart discovery from the beginning because missing evaluation proves that the already agreed business goal and requirement owners must have been incorrect.
options.why: The scenario identifies a skipped lifecycle step rather than invalid requirements, so restarting discovery does not directly complete the missing acceptance work.

options.text: Launch the single-office pilot immediately and count all its responses as acceptance cases, because limited volume makes the agreed security checks optional.
options.why: A smaller population does not waive the owner's explicit pre-pilot gates, particularly unauthorized-access behavior that a happy-path pilot may never expose.

questions.decision: Complete the agreed minimum evaluation and handoff checks before the live pilot, then use pilot monitoring for additional operational learning. A smaller deployment reduces exposure but does not establish the missing evidence. Requirements are already accepted, so the next step is the specified readiness work rather than restarting discovery or treating a polished demo as its substitute.

video_evidence.concept: Evaluation against agreed thresholds must precede handoff and deployment; demonstrations are not acceptance evidence.

questions.title: Retirement belongs to the deployed route
questions.stem: A service uses one Claude route through Amazon Bedrock and a separate direct-provider fallback. A lifecycle spreadsheet tracks only the direct provider's model notices. An operations review finds that route availability also depends on platform-specific model status, region, and account access. The team must retain a controlled upgrade path and cannot assume dates or replacements match across routes. Which THREE practices best turn the chapter's provider-specific retirement lesson into an actionable lifecycle plan?

options.text: Use the direct provider's retirement date for both routes and delete platform notices, because a shared model family guarantees identical hosting lifecycle decisions.
options.why: The chapter and platform guidance distinguish provider schedules, so shared model identity does not establish a common retirement boundary.

options.text: Maintain route-specific model, region, account, lifecycle status, and notice sources, with an owner responsible for checking the platform actually serving each workload.
options.why: The inventory connects lifecycle evidence to deployed dependencies instead of assuming the direct provider's schedule governs every hosting route.

options.text: Evaluate replacement candidates through each intended route, including access, tools, quality, and latency, before treating matching model labels as interchangeable deployments.
options.why: A replacement's name does not establish equivalent route support or task behavior, so migration evidence must cover the actual platform configuration.

options.text: Wait until the first production retirement error to test replacements, assuming the fallback's presence eliminates any need for advance route-specific evaluation.
options.why: An unevaluated fallback may share compatibility or availability problems, and discovering them after retirement removes useful migration and recovery options.

options.text: Set migration checkpoints before each applicable route retirement and rehearse a permitted fallback or rollback while the relevant prior route remains available.
options.why: This converts notices into executable lifecycle actions and avoids planning recovery around a model route that has already become unavailable.

questions.decision: Track each deployed route's platform status and owner, test replacements through that route, and plan migration before its applicable retirement boundary. The direct provider's notices remain relevant to the direct fallback but do not define Bedrock availability. This extends the source lesson from watching another page to maintaining a route-specific, tested transition plan.

video_evidence.concept: Cloud platforms maintain their own model lifecycle schedules, so track the platform actually used.

questions.title: A shared plugin declaration is not completed enrollment
questions.stem: A development team wants a consistent Claude Code plugin containing skills, hooks, and an MCP server. The organization permits a private marketplace, and the documented configuration supports project-scoped marketplace and enabled-plugin declarations. New team members currently copy instructions from a wiki and sometimes omit components. Security still requires repository trust and approved plugin provenance. Which TWO changes best improve reproducible team setup without claiming that a committed declaration silently bypasses trust or installation behavior?

options.text: Test setup from a clean team account, recording required trust or enrollment steps and verifying the expected skill, hook, and MCP components actually load.
options.why: This checks the deployed result and preserves the stated trust boundary rather than equating a committed configuration entry with completed installation on every client.

options.text: Paste all plugin files into project instructions and assume the runtime interprets instruction prose as installed hooks and configured MCP connections.
options.why: Project instructions provide context, but copying plugin code there does not establish the executable plugin components and connections required by the team.

options.text: Commit the approved marketplace and enabled-plugin declarations in the supported project settings, pinning or governing the reviewed plugin source according to team policy.
options.why: The repository provides a reproducible shared setup reference instead of relying on each developer to recreate the intended components manually.

options.text: Disable repository trust prompts globally so committed declarations can install any future marketplace addition without provenance checks or explicit enrollment behavior.
options.why: This bypasses the stated trust and provenance requirement and mistakes friction removal for a reproducible, approved setup process.

options.text: Use each developer's private user settings as the only source of truth and remove the repository declarations to avoid any shared setup review.
options.why: Uncoordinated private copies recreate the manual drift that motivated the task and make the intended team configuration harder to inspect.

questions.decision: Commit the supported project declarations and verify a clean member's enrollment, trust, and resulting components. A declarative team configuration reduces manual drift but is not evidence that every client has installed or trusted the plugin. This qualifies the video's automatic-sharing shorthand with an actual setup check and a preserved provenance boundary.

video_evidence.concept: Share approved plugin marketplace and enabled-plugin configuration through project settings, respecting trust and enrollment behavior.

questions.title: Compute the effective permission result
questions.stem: A Claude Code rollout review supplies the effective matching rules in the exhibit. Managed policy remains authoritative, and the documented evaluation order is deny, then ask, then allow. Every listed match is stipulated valid, so command-pattern syntax is not in dispute. The reviewer must identify what developers will experience before the preview workflow is enabled. Which conclusion correctly evaluates all three operations without assuming the most specific allow overrides a matching deny or ask rule?

options.text: Preview publishing is denied, reading the release draft asks, and reading the local guide is allowed under the stipulated matching rules.
options.why: Deny precedes the preview allow, ask precedes the draft allow, and the guide has no higher-priority matching rule blocking its project allow.

options.text: Preview publishing is denied, while both reads ask because any organization with managed settings must confirm every operation matched by a project allowance.
options.why: The managed denial is scoped to its matching operation; the stipulated guide path has only an allow and does not acquire an unstated confirmation requirement.

options.text: All three operations are allowed because project rules are more specific than general user or managed rules whenever the commands differ by purpose.
options.why: Specificity does not reverse the stipulated deny-ask-allow order, and managed policy cannot be displaced by a conflicting project allowance.

options.text: Preview publishing asks, reading the release draft is allowed, and reading the local guide is denied because conflicting rules cancel into confirmation.
options.why: The documented order resolves matches directly; conflicts do not cancel into a prompt, and no matching denial is supplied for the local guide.

questions.decision: Preview publishing is denied, reading the release draft asks, and reading the local guide is allowed. Resolve the effective matches in their documented order rather than by apparent specificity. This extends the chapter’s deny-precedence lesson to a complete rollout table, where an ask rule also remains decisive ahead of an allow rule.

video_evidence.concept: Deny rules precede ask and allow; a narrower local allow cannot override a matching managed denial.

questions.title: A failing test must fail for the right reason
questions.stem: A team asks Claude Code to fix a timestamp parser whose specification rejects impossible calendar dates. The agent first writes a failing test, but it fails because the fixture file cannot be found, not because the parser accepts an impossible date. Implementation work then makes the suite green by creating the fixture, leaving the parser defect untouched. Which workflow correction BEST applies test-first discipline without treating any initial red result as an adequate behavioral oracle?

options.text: Accept the first red result as sufficient test-first evidence and count fixture creation as the complete parser repair once the suite turns green.
options.why: The test never demonstrated the wrong parser behavior, so its color change cannot establish that impossible dates are now rejected.

options.text: Add many successful ordinary-date tests after the fixture repair and infer invalid-date correctness from higher passing coverage on the unchanged parser.
options.why: Ordinary success coverage does not exercise the rejection boundary, so it cannot substitute for a test that distinguishes the known invalid-date defect.

options.text: Repair the fixture setup, verify the old parser fails the specific invalid-date assertion, then implement the parser change while keeping the independently reviewed expectation fixed.
options.why: This establishes that the test actually detects the behavioral defect before the implementation changes, rather than merely exercising an unrelated setup error.

options.text: Change the expected result to whatever the existing parser returns, preserving the red-green sequence by adjusting the fixture until the test passes.
options.why: This makes the oracle follow the defect and loses the independently specified calendar behavior that the test is supposed to protect.

questions.decision: Make the test assert the specified invalid-date rejection, confirm the intended assertion fails on the old parser, then implement and review the repair. A missing fixture is an infrastructure failure, not evidence that the test distinguishes correct parsing from the bug. The chapter's test-first lesson therefore includes checking why the red stage is red.

video_evidence.concept: Test-first work establishes expected behavior before implementation and must verify the intended failure mechanism.

questions.title: A retry can be an experiment, not the repair
questions.stem: An integration test intermittently observes an empty index after a background import. Adding a retry usually makes it pass, and developers propose closing the bug. Logs show no correlation between import-completion events and the first query. The expected contract says queries start only after a committed import, and a controlled scheduler can pause either worker.
